scope.topic: Mitosis: duplicated chromosome alignment and sister chromatid separation in eukaryotic cells
scope.organism_context: eukaryotic cells (animal cell examples with centrosomes/centrioles; plant/fungi differences noted but not modeled)
included_processes: prometaphase kinetochore attachment and chromosome orientation
metaphase alignment at the metaphase plate
anaphase sister chromatid separation and poleward movement
excluded_processes: prophase nuclear envelope breakdown and centrosome separation
simplifications: Only one duplicated chromosome (one sister chromatid pair) is modeled; the source's 'all chromosomes' statements are instantiated for this single pair only. The alignment observable checks that this one modeled duplicated chromosome is at the metaphase plate, explicitly delimiting it as an instantiation of the universal source statement.

Separation is represented by the joined sister-chromatid pair splitting into two distinct persistent daughter chromatid entities (each now called a chromosome), each moving toward an opposite pole. The post-separation identity is carried by these two daughter chromatid entities, not by the whole pair.

The molecular mechanism by which the sister-chromatid connection breaks down (cohesin degradation/cleavage) is not modeled; only the observable breakdown of the connection is asserted, and no causal sufficiency of microtubule pulling alone is claimed.
Processes are discrete stages for schematic clarity; the after/concurrent_with links represent schematic phase order, not strict per-chromosome mechanistic causal prerequisites.
Maximal chromosome condensation at metaphase is noted in source but excluded from process effects as out-of-scope for alignment/separation proof.

observable_reviews.reason: Source explicitly states mitotic spindle microtubules from opposite poles attach to each sister chromatid at the kinetochore; model's relation and during-prometaphase scope match this entailment, and participant identities (kinetochore on each sister chromatid, microtubules from opposite poles) are preserved.

Source states all chromosomes are aligned at the metaphase plate during metaphase; model explicitly delimits its single-chromosome instantiation as a schematic instantiation of the universal statement, so the narrow observable is source-supported without overclaiming completeness.

Source describes anaphase connection breakdown and poleward pulling in sequence after metaphase alignment; the model marks this as schematic phase order rather than strict per-chromosome causal prerequisite, preserving the source's observable order without adding unsupported causal sufficiency.

Source states each chromatid, now called a chromosome, is pulled toward the centrosome to which its microtubule is attached; the model's state transition to two distinct daughter chromatid entities moving to opposite poles matches this identity change and movement without modeling the excluded molecular mechanism.

review.scope_review: The model's scope is explicitly bounded to one duplicated chromosome in a eukaryotic (animal-cell example) context, with interphase replication, prophase events, telophase, cytokinesis, spindle assembly checkpoint regulation, and molecular cohesin degradation/cleavage excluded. Included processes—prometaphase bipolar kinetochore attachment/orientation, metaphase alignment, and anaphase sister separation with poleward movement—are directly supported by the source excerpts. Simplifications are honest: single-chromosome instantiation is flagged against the source's 'all chromosomes' statement; daughter chromatid identity is carried by post-separation entities; molecular mechanism of connection breakdown is not asserted as modeled; discrete stages are marked as schematic phase order rather than strict causal prerequisites; maximal condensation is noted but excluded from proof. No fully formal but biologically false claim is present, and the schematic does not overclaim to prove molecular chemistry. Unresolved questions appropriately flag timing, checkpoint requirement, and strict precondition status. No blocking issues identified.

scope.topic: Skeletal muscle excitation-contraction-relaxation at the level of a single vertebrate skeletal muscle fibre
scope.organism_context: Vertebrate skeletal muscle fibre (fast-twitch/general skeletal fibre); cardiac and insect muscle excluded
included_processes: Excitation of the skeletal muscle fibre by motor neuron acetylcholine leading to sarcolemma and T-tubule depolarization
SR Ca2+ release into the sarcoplasm
Ca2+ binding to troponin and exposure of myosin-binding sites on actin
ATP-dependent cross-bridge cycling and thin-filament sliding (contraction)
Cessation of ACh release, repolarization, SR Ca2+ reuptake and reshielding of actin-binding sites (relaxation)
excluded_processes: Molecular atomic detail of myosin ATPase and actin-myosin interfaces
ATP regeneration pathways (creatine phosphate, glycolysis, aerobic respiration) beyond noting ATP requirement
Muscle fatigue mechanisms and oxygen debt details
simplifications: Nervous system circuitry upstream of the motor neuron terminal is not modelled.
Ca2+ is treated as a single sarcoplasmic pool rather than distinct SR subcompartments.
The repeated cross-bridge cycle is represented as one process rather than individual stroke events.
Fast-twitch-specific regulators such as MCARE/SERCA1 modulation are noted but not required for the general vertebrate skeletal fibre mechanism.

processes.scientific_name: ATP-dependent cross-bridge cycling and thin-filament sliding

temporal_scope.start_condition: Actin-binding sites exposed and ATP available
temporal_scope.end_condition: Ca2+ removed or ATP depleted (contraction ceases)

support.quote: As long as Ca ++ ions remain in the sarcoplasm to bind to troponin, which keeps the actin-binding sites “unshielded,” and as long as ATP is available to drive the cross-bridge cycling and the pulling of actin strands by myosin, the muscle fiber will continue to shorten to an anatomical limit.

This allows the myosin heads to bind to these exposed binding sites and form cross-bridges. The thin filaments are then pulled by the myosin heads to slide past the thick filaments toward the center of the sarcomere.
ATP binding causes the myosin head to detach from the actin ( Figure 10.11 d ). After this occurs, ATP is converted to ADP and P i by the intrinsic ATPase activity of myosin.

exceptions.description: If ATP runs out, myosin heads cannot detach from actin and the muscle cannot relax normally (rigor).
exceptions.evidence_quote: In the absence of ATP, the myosin head will not detach from actin.

support.quote: Muscle contraction usually stops when signaling from the motor neuron ends, which repolarizes the sarcolemma and T-tubules, and closes the voltage-gated calcium channels in the SR. Ca ++ ions are then pumped back into the SR, which causes the tropomyosin to reshield (or re-cover) the binding sites on the actin strands.
Relaxing skeletal muscle fibers, and ultimately, the skeletal muscle, begins with the motor neuron, which stops releasing its chemical signal, ACh, into the synapse at the NMJ.
Muscle contraction usually stops when signaling from the motor neuron ends, which repolarizes the sarcolemma and T-tubules, and closes the voltage-gated calcium channels in the SR.

ATP-driven pumps will move Ca ++ out of the sarcoplasm back into the SR. This results in the “reshielding” of the actin-binding sites on the thin filaments. Without the ability to form cross-bridges between the thin and thick filaments, the muscle fiber loses its tension and relaxes.

exceptions.description: A muscle may also stop contracting when it runs out of ATP and becomes fatigued.
exceptions.evidence_quote: A muscle also can stop contracting when it runs out of ATP and becomes fatigued ( Figure 10.9 ).
